title: Whole-of-state defense: How SLED agencies can secure critical infrastructure in the AI era
content_md: AI is widening the attack surface of the critical infrastructure facilities and services that state, local, and education (SLED) organizations run. In the final post of our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series, we explain how a whole-of-state security approach can help SLED agencies protect their critical infrastructure. Key takeaways Because cyber attackers prey on under-resourced targets, they often go after SLED organizations, especially those that operate critical infrastructure, including water systems, hospitals, mass transit, emergency services, and schools. In the latest research from the National Association of State Chief Information Officers (NASCIO), nearly 90% of state CIOs rated cyberattacks on critical systems as a high concern. AI expands the attack surface in two fundamental ways: SLED agencies and employees adopt AI tools and AI-built apps faster than security teams can authorize and inventory them, while attackers use AI automation to find weak points faster. A whole-of-state cybersecurity approach treats state agencies, counties, cities, school districts, and utilities as one defensive perimeter, with shared visibility, shared services, and clear governance. Cyber attackers often look for the weakest link that can offer them an entry point into larger targets. If they can’t crack a state agency’s hardened systems, they’ll try to breach it in a roundabout way by first breaking into a small town’s water utility, a rural school district, or a county dispatch
